analysis.one_liner: Requires large employers to offer family health coverage and pay a share of premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: introduced May 2005 with no cosponsors, it sat in five House committees until the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal labor law to require every employer with 50 or more full-time workers to offer a family health plan at least as good as the standard federal employee plan, and to pay the same share of premiums the federal government pays for its own workers (about three-quarters). Workers would pay the rest through payroll withholding; employers that refused could face civil penalties. It never moved past committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large firms, including part-timers, contract workers, and uninsured family members, who would gain guaranteed access to employer-sponsored family coverage with a substantial employer contribution. Also Medicaid/Medicare enrollees who work would be shifted to employer coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Requires large employers to offer every employee a family health plan at least as valuable as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan available to federal employees, with coverage starting within 30 days of hire.
Requires the employer to pay at least the same share of premiums the federal government pays for the federal employee plan, so workers get meaningful help with the cost.
Counts contract workers as employees and prorates the employer contribution for part-timers, so firms cannot avoid the mandate by using contractors or short hours.
Enforces the mandate through civil money penalties and injunctions, and lets states adopt stricter coverage requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers, who would bear a new premium contribution for every employee and family member; health insurers would face new minimum-benefit standards; federal programs like Medicare and Medicaid would pay some workers' premium shares.

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate raises the cost of hiring, which economists and employers warned could reduce hiring or push firms to keep headcount under 50.
Workers bear the employee share of premiums through payroll withholding, and employers could offset the mandate through lower wages.
The bill sets no small-group or individual options for workers at firms under 50 employees, leaving millions of uninsured people uncovered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For uninsured workers and families at large firms, guaranteed employer-paid coverage is a large, direct benefit. The cost is a new employer mandate whose burden can fall back on workers through wages or reduced hiring, and it does nothing for the uninsured at smaller firms. Its quality benchmark (the FEHBP standard plan) is a real, concrete floor rather than a vague one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to five House committees and then to several subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Referred to the Education and the Workforce, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services committees on May 5, 2005.
Subsequently referred to subcommittees on Health, Employer-Employee Relations, Workforce Protections, and Military Personnel through June 2005; no further action followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers kept the status quo, with no new obligation to offer or help pay for family health coverage. Uninsured workers and their families gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers avoiding a coverage mandate

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member

for.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the referral and its Health and Employer-Employee Relations subcommittees took no action on the bill.

against.name: House committee chairs of the 109th Congress
against.role: Chairs of the five committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors joined the Democratic sponsor, and the Republican-led House never acted on the bill.

industries.note: They would have had to offer qualifying family coverage and pay a fixed share of premiums, a new benefit cost they did not previously owe to all workers.
The bill mandates minimum benefit value equal to the federal employee standard plan, raising standards, but also guarantees a pool of employer-sponsored customers at large firms.
